chief_complaint: painless deep plantar ulcer under first metatarsal head
hpi_details: A 68-year-old woman with diabetes presents with a painless deep plantar ulcer beneath the first metatarsal head, with reduced protective sensation suspected.
ideas: She thinks the hole under the ball of her foot is just a burst friction blister or an open callus from walking in stiff new garden shoes.
concerns: She is worried that the sore might reach the bone and lead to an amputation like her brother went through.
expectations: She hopes to receive a strong antibiotic ointment and sterile bandages so the skin can close up quickly.
pmh: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy

clinical_knowledge.topic: Diabetic Foot Ulcer evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Diabetic Foot Ulcer is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Diabetic Foot Ulcer: Wound debridement, off-loading footwear, check arterial flow, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: painless deep plantar ulcer under first metatarsal head
Key HPI features: A painless deep plantar ulcer beneath the first metatarsal head in a patient with diabetes, concerning for neuropathic ulceration.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Diabetic Foot Ulcer.
Relevant background/PMH: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with peripheral neuropathy
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Diabetic Foot Ulcer.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Soft tissue infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Missing limb-threatening infection, critical ischemia, or osteomyelitis before debridement and off-loading.
management_principles: Plan for Diabetic Foot Ulcer: Wound debridement, off-loading footwear, check arterial flow
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of painless deep plantar ulcer under first metatarsal head. HPI: neuropathy, repetitive pressure.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Diabetic Foot Ulcer.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Diabetic Foot Ulcer.
reference_soap.plan: Assess urgently for infection, ischemia, and osteomyelitis. Debride nonviable tissue when appropriate, provide effective off-loading, assess arterial perfusion, optimize glycemic control, and involve a multidisciplinary diabetic-foot service.

red_flags: Fever, rapidly spreading erythema, purulence, crepitus, severe pain, or systemic illness requiring same-day emergency evaluation
Cool or pale foot, absent pulses, gangrene, or rapidly progressive ulceration suggesting critical ischemia

must_ask.objective: Duration and progression of the ulcer
must_ask.say: How long has this ulcer been there, and has it gotten deeper?
Can you feel this ulcer at all, or is your foot numb?
How long have you had diabetes, and how well controlled is your blood sugar?
Is there any redness, swelling, drainage, or odor from the wound?
What kind of shoes do you wear, and have you been keeping weight off that foot?

history.answer: I noticed an open sore on the bottom of my right foot about three weeks ago, and it just isn't healing.
I don't recall any specific cut or injury, but there was a thick, hardened callus in that spot for months that eventually broke open.
I first noticed the open sore about three weeks ago, and it has gradually grown slightly wider rather than closing up.
It is located on the sole of my right foot right under the base of my big toe, roughly the size of a coin, and it looks like a deep crater.
No, I haven't stepped on any rusty nails, glass, or foreign objects, and no animals or pets have bitten or scratched me.
It hasn't had heavy or spurting bleeding at all, just a bit of clear watery fluid and occasional faint spots of blood on my socks.
My feet have felt numb and tingly like I'm wearing thick socks for a few years now, but I can still move and wiggle my toes normally.
No, I haven't burned my foot with hot water, hot packs, or heating pads, and I haven't been near any chemicals or fire.
Surprisingly, it doesn't hurt at all, even when I stand on it, press directly around it, or walk.
It has been open for three weeks, and all I've done is wash it with plain tap water and put a regular adhesive bandage over it every morning.
No, I haven't noticed any spreading redness, warmth, bad smell, or thick yellow pus coming from the sore.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, sweating, or feelings of being sick.
I walk around my house and do light housework every day, so I'm definitely not bedridden or sitting down all day long.
I don't get any calf cramping or tightness when I walk, and my feet don't usually feel freezing cold or painful when resting in bed.
I had a tetanus booster shot about eight years ago after scraping my arm while gardening.
I don't take any blood thinners or steroids, and as far as I know, my immune system is normal.
No, this is definitely not from any physical violence, abuse, or intentional self-harm.
I was told I had type 2 diabetes about twelve years ago, but I haven't been taking diabetes pills regularly or checking my blood sugars for over a year.
I usually wear flat slip-on shoes or walk barefoot inside my house, and I haven't been using any special cushioned insoles or custom shoes.
I don't have any swelling in my legs, bulging veins, or brownish skin discoloration around my ankles.
I figured a blister from my stiff new walking shoes must have popped and opened up without me noticing it.
I saw my brother lose his foot after a sore got out of hand, and I'm terrified this will end in an amputation.
I was hoping you could prescribe a strong healing ointment and bandage it up so it heals quickly on its own.
Other than my diabetes and the nerve numbness in my feet, I don't have any other chronic medical illnesses.
I have never had any surgeries and I have never been admitted to a hospital.
I am not currently taking any prescribed medications, over-the-counter pills, or health supplements.
I don't have any known allergies to medications, foods, or bandages.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I only drink a glass of wine socially once or twice a month, and nothing more than that.
I am retired, and I live with my husband in a quiet single-story house.
My mother had diabetes and high blood pressure, but no one in my family ever needed an amputation or had serious foot ulcers.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg, pulse 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Well-nourished, comfortable 68-year-old female in no acute distress, sitting comfortably without grimacing.

A 1.5 cm round, punched-out deep ulcer under the right first metatarsal head surrounded by a thick callus, with a clean pink granulation base, no exposed tendon or bone on gentle probing, and no surrounding erythema, fluctuance, crepitus, or purulent drainage.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally, feet are warm to touch, and capillary refill time is under 2 seconds in all toes.

Loss of protective sensation to Semmes-Weinstein 10-gram monofilament across the plantar surfaces bilaterally in a stocking distribution, with diminished vibration sense at the first metatarsophalangeal joints.
Motor strength is 5/5 in bilateral toe flexion, toe extension, ankle dorsiflexion, and ankle plantarflexion.
Achilles tendon reflexes are absent bilaterally, while patellar reflexes are 1+ bilaterally.
No pitting edema, hemosiderin pigmentation, venous varicosities, or stasis changes on either lower extremity.
Both calves are soft, non-tender, and symmetrical without swelling or palpable cords.
Full range of motion in bilateral ankles and metatarsophalangeal joints without swelling, warmth, or deformity.
